text: My brother and I work at the same architecture firm — small place, maybe ten people. I was going through shared project files for a residential reno and noticed he's logged about twelve hours he clearly didn't work over the last two months. The client is a family friend, someone who's known us since we were kids. We're talking maybe three or four hundred dollars total. I haven't said anything and honestly I don't think I'm going to. He's my little brother, he's twenty-two, he's probably not even thinking of it as stealing — just rounding up his hours because he's underpaid and overworked. If I bring it up it becomes this whole thing: my parents get involved, the firm gets involved, the client finds out, and over what? A few hundred bucks that the client probably won't even notice on the final invoice. I just want to know if I'm being reasonable here or if I'm overthinking it and should just move on with my life.

My brother and I work at the same architecture firm. He's younger than me, I basically raised him after our mom left, and I got him the job here. He's been doing structural calculations on a mid-rise residential project that's already halfway built, and I found out last week that he's been signing off on load figures he knows are under what the engineering spec calls for. He told me he did it to keep the project on budget and that the margins are wide enough that it's not actually dangerous. I want to believe him. He's not stupid, he's not careless, he just got pressured on timeline and cost and made a judgment call. I haven't said anything to anyone else. Part of me thinks if I just talk to him privately and give him a chance to quietly fix the numbers before the next review cycle, nobody gets hurt and the building is fine. If I go to the project lead, he's done. Not just fired — probably blacklisted, maybe legal trouble. And my family will never forgive me. Our dad is already sick and this would kill him. I keep thinking about how I'm the one who got him this job, so in a way this is my responsibility too. Am I being crazy for wanting to handle this between us? He said he'll fix it. Should I just give him the time?

My mum's been admitted to hospital after a fall and I need to get there now. I'm a dental nurse and I was supposed to stay for a procedure this afternoon — patient with severe phobia, already cancelled three times. My colleague is telling me I need to do a handover or something before I walk out and I honestly can't believe I'm even being asked. My mother is in hospital. Can I just leave?

So I did the inspection on Thursday and the heating's been out for three weeks now. Three weeks. The tenant's got two kids, one's four and one's seven, and the older one's got this chesty cough that's clearly been getting worse and the mum looked absolutely exhausted and the flat was freezing, like you could see your breath. I filed the maintenance report the same day and I've sent two follow-ups to the landlord but he's in Thailand or somewhere and his phone's off and the letting agreement says I need written authorisation before I can instruct a contractor. I know that's what it says. I know. But I keep thinking about those kids and it's been three weeks already and if I wait for him to come back online that's another four or five days minimum, probably more because he's not great at responding even when he's reachable. I could get a plumber out tomorrow, I know one who'd do it, and just invoice the landlord after. But if he kicks off about it or says the work wasn't necessary or the cost was too high, that comes out of my pocket or I get disciplined for going outside procedure. I've been at this agency two years and I can't afford to lose this job. But I also can't stop thinking about that kid coughing. What do I actually do here?

I went ahead and called a boiler engineer without landlord sign-off. Kids were sick, heating had been out three weeks, landlord unreachable overseas. Now he's back and saying I had no right to commit him to the cost without asking. Am I in the wrong here or is he just being a prick?

I reported my brother to his supervisor at the library where we both work and now my whole family is treating me like I committed a crime. He was taking photos of patron IDs during registration — names, addresses, birth dates — and keeping them on a tablet we share at home. I found them by accident. I told my manager the next morning. Now he's been suspended and they're talking about pressing charges, and my mom called me at 2am crying saying I ruined his life over nothing, that he was just curious, that he didn't even sell the information or whatever. And I keep thinking maybe she's right. Maybe I overreacted. He's 22. He's my little brother. I could have just talked to him first, told him to delete them, given him a chance to fix it himself. Instead I went straight over his head and now there might be a police report with his name on it. Did I do the wrong thing? I can't sleep. I keep replaying it and thinking I should have handled it differently, just between us, and maybe the patrons were never actually in danger because he never did anything with the photos.

I'm the first-aider at a junior football club. There's a 15-year-old I'm fairly certain has a stress fracture. I told the coach after a session and he basically told me to do one. I put it in writing to the secretary like our procedure says, but the committee doesn't meet for nearly two weeks and the kid trains three times a week in the meantime. So last Tuesday I pulled him from the session and messaged his mum to explain why. Now the coach is going around saying I've gone over everyone's head and caused drama, and a couple of the committee members have made comments about me not following process. I keep going back and forth on whether I should have just waited it out. Was I wrong to step in like that?

My mum raised me on her own from when I was nine, worked two jobs, never asked anyone for anything. When she mentioned she wanted to put herself forward for treasurer at our allotment committee I told her I'd nominate her and back her at the AGM. That was before I found out from the current treasurer — who's leaving and asked me to keep this between us — that a few years back when mum was assistant treasurer, some small amounts went missing from the petty cash. We're talking maybe forty, fifty pounds over a whole season. She's not a criminal, she was probably just disorganised, and that was four years ago. She's done everything for me my whole life and I gave her my word. I keep going back and forth but honestly I feel like pulling out now would be the cruel thing, not the principled thing. She'd know something was up and she'd never get the chance to find out why. Is it really worth wrecking that over a few quid from years ago?

I've decided I'm not going to nominate my mum for treasurer. I need to tell her before the meeting in six weeks. The problem is I can't say why without throwing the outgoing treasurer under the bus, and I gave them my word I wouldn't. How do I pull out of supporting her without giving a reason that leads to follow-up questions she'll eventually answer correctly?

Marcus and I have been on the same team for about two years now and we get along fine, we cover each other's lunches, that kind of thing. But I've been watching him close applications as withdrawn when people miss one phone appointment. The procedure says you're supposed to send a follow-up letter giving them another chance before you do that. He's not breaking any written rule exactly - the system lets you close it that way - but the whole point of the letter is that these people are often chaotic, they miss calls because they're in crisis, they don't have stable phone access. Three people this month have lost their queue position and had to start over. That's weeks of their life.

I keep going back and forth on what to do. Part of me thinks I should just flag it to our team lead because honestly the thought of sitting Marcus down and saying "hey I've been watching what you do" makes me feel physically sick. We work next to each other every day. If I make it weird between us I still have to sit there for eight hours. And he's not a bad person, he's just cutting corners because the queue is long and he's stressed. Maybe I should just let the team lead handle it since it's kind of a process issue anyway.

But then I also wonder if I'm making too much of it. Like, is it actually my job to monitor how he processes his caseload? We're the same grade. Nobody put me in charge of quality checking him. Maybe I should just mind my own applications and stop losing sleep over this.

So what do I actually do here? Do I go to the team lead, or am I overthinking the whole thing?

Marcus trained me when I started at the housing benefits office two years ago and honestly he's been really good to me. He's the one who showed me how everything works, covered for me when I was still slow, that kind of thing. But lately I've noticed he's been closing applications as 'withdrawn' when people miss a single phone appointment, instead of sending the follow-up letter that's supposed to give them another shot. Three people this month have lost their queue position because of it and had to start their claims over from scratch. I keep going back and forth on whether to say anything. Part of me thinks maybe I should just document what I've seen and bring it up with the department head, because at least then it's not me confronting him directly and I don't have to worry about how he'll take it from someone he trained. But then I also wonder if I'm just making excuses because I'm scared of the conversation. He's senior to me. He's the one who basically decided I was competent enough to stay. Am I really the person who gets to tell him he's doing something wrong? The applicants are losing time they can't get back, I know that. But it's not like he's breaking a rule exactly, he's just using a gap. Maybe I'm overthinking it and it's genuinely not my problem to solve.

So I ran a quarterly review on our claims team and found that Gerald — he's been here fourteen years, trains every new hire, everyone on the team goes to him when they're stuck — approved eleven claims that skipped the eligibility verification step. Not fraud, nothing like that. The claimants were probably fine, he probably just used his judgment and moved them through. The verification step is honestly kind of a checkbox thing that was added after a compliance audit three years ago and half the team finds it annoying anyway.

Here's what's eating at me: if I flag this formally, it goes on his record. He's 58. He's the person who stayed late to help me when I first got promoted into this role and had no idea what I was doing. The team morale would tank — people genuinely look up to him and I think some of them would see me as the one who turned on him over a technicality.

But also I'm the one who found it. If I don't do anything and it comes up in an external audit later, that's on me.

I keep going back and forth. Part of me thinks I should just pull him aside and say hey, can you double-check the verification step going forward, no big deal, and leave it at that. Part of me thinks even that's overreacting because honestly the claims were probably legitimate and the process is just the process.

What do I actually do here? Do I write it up? Do I just talk to him informally? Do I let it go and tighten up the process going forward without naming what happened?

I've decided to pull Gerald aside about the claims thing. How do I bring it up without it sounding like I'm accusing him of something? He's going to take it personally no matter what I say and I don't want him to think I'm questioning his judgment after everything he's done for this team. What are the actual words I should use?

My cousin has been funneling repair contracts to his buddy's company at like 40% markup for over a year and I just found the paper trail. The work quality has been sliding the whole time and last month a balcony railing his guy signed off on collapsed and a tenant is in the hospital with a broken pelvis. I handle all the finances and contracts for our property management business so this is partially on me for not catching it sooner. I need to pull him off the role and make sure the injury gets reported properly, but here's the thing — we coordinate everything through a family WhatsApp group. Him, me, my two siblings, our mom. If I bring it up there she's going to take his side and the whole family splits. I've been making excuses for him for months, telling myself the quality drop was just bad luck or supply issues. I'm so done making excuses. But I keep thinking about my mom, she's already dealing with her own health stuff and this is going to wreck her. Do I just do it? Do I talk to him privately first and then bring it to the group after? Is there any way to handle this without becoming the person who broke the family apart?

I've already decided to remove my cousin from his maintenance role in our family property business. He's been overcharging us through a friend's firm for over a year and a tenant got seriously hurt because of the declining work quality. I need to post this in our family group chat — him, my two siblings, and my mom are all in it. How do I word the message so it's firm and factual without sounding like a personal attack? I want my mom to see that this is about a tenant in the hospital, not about me holding a grudge.

I've already decided I'm going to flag the allergy field corruption in standup — I can't sit on it while patient data is getting mangled. But Marcus designed that module and he's been here forever and everyone respects him, and I keep going back and forth on how to actually say it without making him feel like I'm ambushing him in front of the whole team. I don't want him to get defensive and dig in, I need him to help fix this fast. Should I frame it as something I noticed in the logs rather than pointing at his deploy directly? Is there a way to raise it that keeps him on my side instead of making him feel blindsided?

So my friend Amara just walked into the shop where I work and she's basically falling apart. Her phone got water damaged this morning and she has a remote court hearing this afternoon — like a custody hearing, her ex is trying to take the kids — and if her phone doesn't work she can't join the call and it could go really badly for her. There are four people ahead of her in the queue and our boss is out today so it's just me running the floor. I know the policy is first come first served and I get that, but those four people are probably just here for screen replacements or battery swaps, nothing that's going to ruin someone's life if they wait an extra twenty minutes. Amara is literally shaking. I keep thinking about what happens if I don't help her and she loses this hearing. Can I just pull her in? I feel like I'd be failing her if I made her sit in the waiting area for an hour while I do someone's iPad screen.

Six files. I've gone back through them three times now and the pattern is obvious—scores bumped up for applicants whose families are connected to one of the university's biggest donors. The person doing it is Tomás. He's been my mentor for two years. He literally put my name forward for this position when it opened up, coached me through the interview, sat with me the first week when I didn't know what I was doing. I wouldn't be here without him. That's not an exaggeration.

The decision round closes in three days. I don't have a supervisor I trust enough to go to, and there's no anonymous hotline or anything like that. If I say something, it goes straight to people who will act on it, and he loses his job. Not just gets a warning—loses it. The kind of thing that follows you.

And here's what I keep coming back to: those applicants who'd get displaced, they're applying to other schools too. They're not going to end up with nothing. They'll land somewhere. But Tomás—if this comes out, his career in this field is over. He's in his fifties. He's not going to bounce back from a termination for cause.

I keep telling myself maybe I'm wrong, maybe I'm reading the scores wrong, but I've checked the rubric against the files and I'm not wrong. I know what I'm seeing.

So I guess what I'm asking is—am I actually obligated to do something here? Because I keep reading about how you're supposed to report stuff like this but nobody talks about what it costs the person who reports. I gave him two years of trust. He gave me a career. Is it really fair that I'm supposed to burn that down over six files when the people affected have other options?

I've decided to report it. That part's done in my head. What I can't figure out is whether I tell him first or just go straight to the department chair. If I tell him first he'll have time to spin it or destroy the files. If I don't tell him, he finds out from someone else and it looks like I stabbed him in the back, which—yeah, maybe I did, but I don't want it to look that way. What do I actually say to the chair? I don't want to sound like I'm doing this for drama. I just need it to sound factual and not like I'm enjoying it.

Dana approved a post that's obviously harassment — same user getting targeted across four different threads with slurs and I can't believe she let it through. We have a shared decision log where corrections go and I want to flag it there with the full reasoning so the rest of the team can see what the policy actually requires. She's my closest friend on the team, five years, but honestly I'm past the point of giving her a pass because of that. She's been sloppy for months and I keep quietly fixing things behind the scenes. I want to post the correction today, publicly, where everyone can see it. Should I just do it or is there some reason I shouldn't?

I've decided to flag Dana's bad call in the shared decision log. She approved a post that's clearly harassment under our policy — repeated derogatory comments targeting one user across multiple threads. I need help writing the correction entry so it reads as a straightforward policy clarification. I don't want to soften it or make it about her personally, but I also don't want to water down what went wrong.

Dana and I have been friends for three years, we basically built this team together from scratch, and she's the person I trust most to watch my back when upper management gets weird about our metrics. She approved a post today that's clearly targeting one of our users — I can see the pattern across four different threads, it's not even close to ambiguous. The post is still live and I need it down before this escalates. I'm going to bring it up in our one-on-one in twenty minutes. But I'm sitting here trying to figure out how to say it without making her feel like I'm treating her like she's just another moderator who messed up. She's going to take it personally no matter what I say, and honestly she might be right to. We eat lunch together every day. She helped me through my divorce last year. How do I tell her this was a serious miss without making it sound like our friendship is conditional on her performance?

Dana approved a post that violates our harassment policy. I could just quietly pull it myself and not say anything to her. She's my closest friend on the team and I really don't want to damage that over a moderation call. Should I just handle it silently or do I actually need to bring it up with her directly?

Marcus has been volunteering at our church food distribution for years — longer than most of the council members. Three weeks ago they switched to this new registration system where people have to sign up publicly at the front of the hall and wait in a visible queue while their details get checked. Since then Marcus has gotten really harsh with people. Rushing them, talking loudly about their paperwork, making comments that clearly embarrass them. A few of the regulars who were already in fragile situations have just stopped showing up.

Here's the thing though — I'm not on the council. I don't have any official role. I just help out on Thursdays. The council made this system, and it's the system that's creating the pressure that's making Marcus act this way. If I go to him, what am I actually going to say? 'Hey, stop being mean to people'? He's going to say the system is broken and he's right. And if I go to the council, I'm basically throwing a fellow volunteer under the bus over something that's really a structural problem they created.

I keep thinking the right move is to just raise the system issue at the next open meeting — suggest they go back to the old way or at least make registration less public. That way I'm not pointing fingers at anyone, I'm just addressing the root cause. Does that seem reasonable or am I overthinking this?

I promised a parent I wouldn't tell anyone and now I'm sitting here watching her kid flinch every time someone raises their voice and I can see bruises on her arms and I feel like I'm losing my mind. Three weeks ago this mum came into our office crying and told me her partner had been hitting her in front of their daughter. She was terrified. She said if the school got involved it would make everything worse and she made me swear I wouldn't say anything. I said I wouldn't. I meant it at the time. But since then I've seen the child twice with marks on her arms that look like bruises, and yesterday her teacher told me she's completely withdrawn and flinches when adults get loud. I keep telling myself maybe the mum is handling it, maybe it's not my place, but she's seven. She's seven years old and she's flinching. I think I need to go to our safeguarding lead but I keep going back and forth because I gave my word and this woman trusted me and I'm scared that if I break that promise she'll never trust anyone again and things will actually get worse for her. But then I look at this child and I think what am I even doing keeping a secret that's hurting her? Am I allowed to break a promise when it's a kid's safety? I just need someone to tell me I'm not a terrible person for doing this.

So I've decided I have to say something to my shift partner about the damage reports — I can't keep sitting next to him while he logs scratches that were already there as transit damage, it's been going on for weeks and I'm basically an accessory at this point. But here's the thing, we share a cab five days a week and he's the only reason this job doesn't completely break me. He covered my shifts when my mum was in hospital, he's the one who makes the long hauls bearable. I don't want to come across like I'm reporting him or building a case. I just want him to stop. How do I even bring this up in the truck without it turning into a thing? Do I wait until we're on a quiet stretch? Do I make it about me being uncomfortable rather than about what he's doing wrong? What if he gets defensive and the rest of my shifts become miserable?

I've been working on a revised sorting sequence for the evening shift at our depot for about two months now. I mapped out the full workflow, ran the numbers on throughput, and I'm confident it's an improvement overall. I announced it three weeks out to give everyone time to adjust. Two of our most experienced sorters came back to me almost immediately saying it'll cause more misroutes on oversized parcels. I get that they know the floor better than anyone, but I think they're reacting to the summary I gave them, not the actual design. They haven't seen the full workflow diagram yet. I'm planning a team meeting to walk everyone through it properly so we can all get on the same page before it goes live. Is that the right move? I don't want to just steamroll them but I also don't want to scrap something good because of a knee-jerk reaction.

Meeting's Thursday about the new sorting sequence. I'm the one who said it'll increase misroutes on oversized stuff. I still think that's true. How do I say it in the room without sounding like I'm just being difficult?

I've spent three weeks redesigning the evening sorting sequence at our depot — mapped the full workflow, built exception handling for the oversized lane, ran throughput projections. Posted the one-page summary on the board yesterday and it goes live tomorrow. Within ten minutes two of my senior sorters come up and tell me flat out it's going to increase misroutes on oversized parcels. I respect that they know the floor, but they literally only saw the summary. They haven't seen the diagram, they haven't seen how the oversized exceptions route differently now. I'm running a quick alignment meeting before shift tomorrow to walk through the full picture. How do I structure that so they actually engage with what I'm showing instead of just repeating their initial reaction? I don't want to come across like I'm lecturing them but I also can't throw out three weeks of work because two people had a gut feeling based on a single page.

Coordinator posted a new sorting sequence yesterday, goes live tomorrow. Me and another sorter flagged it'll cause more misroutes on oversized stuff — we've got eleven years between us on that line. Now there's a 'team alignment meeting' before shift. Part of me thinks I should just show up, listen, and let it run for a week so the numbers speak for themselves instead of being the guy who won't get on board. Is that the right call or am I letting it slide?

My brother-in-law works the same shift as me at a delivery app's driver support desk. I found out he's been marking drivers as injured when they're not so they get paid leave. I know for a fact because I saw the approvals in the system — three of them in two weeks, all from the same group of drivers who are clearly not hurt. The thing is, that pool of money is shared, and I've already had two real injury claims delayed because of it. One guy broke his wrist and he's been waiting eleven days.

I want to go straight to my supervisor. I don't want to tip him off. If I say something to him first he's going to either deny it or delete the records, and then I have nothing. Plus honestly I don't think he'd listen to me anyway — he's always been the type who thinks he's smarter than everyone else and that rules are for other people. My sister would be devastated but I can't keep watching real people get screwed over because of him.

Should I just go to my manager tomorrow morning?

I already reported my colleague to the nursing regulator directly, went over my team lead's head, and now I'm not sure I did the right thing. She was falsifying home-visit records — logging appointments that never happened — and patients were genuinely being harmed. One ended up in hospital because an infection went unchecked for over two weeks. So when my team lead told me to wait for an internal review, I couldn't do it. I felt like people were still at risk and waiting was the same as being complicit. But since then I've found out she was carrying almost double the caseload she should have been, and that management had been ignoring her requests for help for months. I keep thinking about how she must have been drowning, and I'm wondering if what I did was disproportionate. I still think the falsification was wrong — I do — but I'm scared I made it about punishing her instead of about protecting patients, and now she might lose her registration over something that was partly a systemic failure. Was I right to go over my team lead's head like that?

This woman keeps showing up on Tuesdays when we only distribute on Thursdays. Third time now. She looks mortified every time and I feel like a jerk telling her to come back. I've got parcels sitting right there. Can I just give her one? It's not like we're running out.

He checks her phone. Not once in a while when she's in the shower—I mean he sits next to her and scrolls through her messages while she's right there, and she just lets him. Last week she cancelled plans with two friends because he said he needed her at home, and when I asked her about it she said it was fine, he was just stressed. I've been watching this for about four months now and it's getting worse.

The thing is, I'm the one on the lease. When they asked if he could move in, I said yes. I said it because she was happy and I wanted her to be happy. Now I want to tell him he has to go. But I said he could stay. I told her he was welcome here and she made plans around that—she bought furniture, she told her friends he was living with us. I don't want to be the person who goes back on what she said.

But I also don't want to sit in my own kitchen and watch my daughter disappear into someone else's schedule. Am I overreacting? Is this just me not liking him and reading too much into things? Or do I actually have grounds to say he needs to find somewhere else?

So I walked the pour today and pulled the rebar schedule against what's actually in the forms on the east section and it's not even close. They skipped every other tie and the spacing on the horizontal bars is way off spec. This is a load-bearing foundation we're talking about. I've been doing this for nineteen years and I have never seen a crew cut corners this badly on structural work. The foreman for that sub was standing right there while they did it, which means either he knew or he wasn't watching, and honestly I don't care which one it is because the result is the same. I want to walk over there tomorrow morning in front of his whole crew and lay it out. Every single deviation, bar by bar, and tell him he's done on this job and I never want to see his company on one of my sites again. I want him to understand what he did and I want everyone else on that site to see what happens when you play games with structural concrete. My project manager is going to tell me to calm down and handle it through the contract but I don't think that's enough. These people could have killed someone. Do I go ahead with what I'm planning or am I overthinking this?

So I've decided I'm going to put one of my processors on a formal improvement plan. She's misclassified overtime rates for our weekend shift category four times now over about two months. Small amounts, we catch them in review before anything goes out, but four times is four times and I can't keep pretending it's a one-off. Here's the thing though — and I haven't told her this or anyone really — the software interface for that category got redesigned about three months ago and nobody on my team got trained on the new layout. Also her workload basically doubled when Marcus left in January and I never backfilled. So I know why she's making the mistakes. I'm not stupid. But I also can't just let it keep happening because eventually one of these is going to slip through review and someone's paycheck is going to be wrong and that's on me. My question is how do I actually have this conversation? Do I bring up the interface change and the workload in the same meeting where I'm telling her she's on a plan, or does that just sound like I'm making excuses for her and then also punishing her? I want her to take it seriously but I also don't want her to walk out of that room thinking I set her up to fail and then blamed her for it. What do I actually say?

Two years I've been working toward this rare-books cataloguing qualification and every single time I get close something comes up. Last year it was the car repair, the year before my mum needed help with a deposit. Now a spot has actually opened on the week-long intensive and registration closes tonight and my colleagues keep saying go for it, and I want to go, I really do, but my mum's behind on rent again and she's got a formal notice. If I pay the fee and take the week unpaid I can't send her what I usually send. She'll probably manage somehow but I don't know. I just keep thinking if I don't take this now there won't be another one for ages and I'll still be shelving paperbacks in five years. Is it selfish to just go for it?

So I've been working my arse off for two years on this electrical installation course, every single practical assessment, I've been in the workshop early, I've done extra practice at home on my own kit, and I came third in the whole cohort. Third. There are four placements with this firm that everyone wants because they actually pay properly and the work is varied, not just pulling cable through conduit for six months. The tutor allocates them based on the rankings, that's literally the stated process, it's in the handbook. I didn't get one. The guy who came seventh got one. Seventh. I was at a mate's barbecue on Saturday and I saw the two of them there together, the tutor and this other student, and they clearly know each other, like properly know each other, not just student-teacher. And now I'm supposed to just sit here and pretend that's a coincidence? The placements get confirmed on Thursday and if I don't do something before then it's done, it's locked in, and I've lost the best opportunity I've had in two years because some bloke knows the tutor from outside. My mates are saying I should go straight to the head of department and name names, say what I saw, say the process is corrupt. Part of me wants to do exactly that. But I also know that if I'm wrong about why he got picked, if there's some other reason I don't know about, I've just accused a member of staff of favouritism and I still have to finish this course and he's still marking my work. So do I go over his head or do I just let it go? Because honestly I can't tell if I'm being rational or if I'm just pissed off and looking for a reason to be pissed off.

I've decided to submit a formal appeal on the placement allocation before Thursday. How do I word it so I'm raising a concern about the selection criteria being applied correctly without directly accusing the tutor of giving someone a favour? I don't have proof of anything dodgy, I just think something's off. I want it to sound like I'm asking for transparency on the process, not like I'm calling him corrupt. What do I actually write?

So I've been volunteering at a drop-in centre for about eight months now, running English conversation classes, and there's this guy Marcus who's been there for six years and basically everyone loves him. He does this weekly session on asylum procedures and he's really good with people, very patient, the attendees trust him. But he's been telling them the wrong deadline for submitting supplementary evidence — the rule changed in January and he never updated, and I only found out because one of the women in my class nearly missed her actual window last week and was panicking about it. I've known about this for three weeks now. I keep telling myself I'll bring it up next session, and then next session comes and I don't. Part of it is that Marcus is the kind of person who takes things really personally and I've seen him get defensive when other volunteers have suggested changes to how he runs things. Part of it is that I'm newer than him and I don't want to be the person who comes in and starts correcting him. But also honestly I just don't want things to get weird between the volunteers because the atmosphere is really good right now and I don't want to be the one who ruins that. The next session is Thursday and I still haven't said anything. Do I actually have to do this or is there some way it could just sort of fix itself?

My younger brother and I are both on staff at a small veterinary clinic here in Napier — there are maybe seven of us all told. A few weeks ago I was pulling together the billing records for a routine surgical case and realized he'd recorded close to ten hours across the past six weeks that he couldn't possibly have worked. The pet belongs to a woman who has been part of our family's life since before I can remember — she and my dad fish together every summer. The overcharge is probably in the range of two hundred dollars, maybe a bit more. I've kept quiet about it and I expect I'll continue to. He's twenty-three and I genuinely don't think he's conscious of it as taking something — more like he's inflating his timesheet because the clinic pays poorly and runs everyone into the ground. The moment I say a word, though, it snowballs: my parents are dragged into it, the head vet finds out, our client learns what happened, and all over what? A sum so small she'd likely never spot it on her account summary. I'm trying to figure out whether I'm handling this sensibly or whether I'm turning a minor thing into a crisis in my head and should just drop it.

I share a workplace with my husband's older brother — we're both at the same pharmaceutical company. He's been there fifteen years, and he's the one who actually recommended me when they were hiring for the QA team. Last week I pulled the batch certification records for a pediatric syrup that's already in distribution, and I realized he's been authorizing purity readings he knows fall below the regulatory threshold. When I confronted him, he said the deviation is small enough that no child is actually at risk, and that pulling the batch would bankrupt the division. Part of me wants to take him at his word. He's meticulous, he's experienced, he just got squeezed on a production deadline and made a call. No one else knows. Some part of me keeps reasoning that if I let him quietly retest and correct the certificates before the next audit, nobody gets harmed and the product is fine. If I escalate this to the compliance director, his career is over. Not just terminated — probably criminally charged, definitely barred from the industry. And my husband would never recover from it. His mother is already in hospice and this would destroy what's left of her. I keep thinking that he's the reason I have this job, so in some way I owe him. Am I deluding myself by wanting to keep this between us? He says he'll correct the records. Should I just give him the window?
